content: Laparoscopy is a widely performed surgical procedure across various specialties. However, complications during laparoscopy often arise during the initial entry into the abdominal cavity. These complications can be life-threatening and include injuries to internal organs such as the bowel or bladder, as well as damage to major blood vessels in the abdominal region. Despite extensive research, there is no consensus on the optimal method for entering the peritoneal cavity during laparoscopy. The objective of this review was to assess the risks and benefits of different laparoscopic entry techniques in both gynecological and non-gynecological surgeries. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared one entry technique to another. The primary outcomes assessed were major complications, including mortality, vascular injuries to major or abdominal wall vessels, injuries to the bladder or bowel, gas embolism, injuries to solid organs, and failed entry into the peritoneal cavity. Secondary outcomes included extraperitoneal insufflation, bleeding or infection at the trocar site, incisional hernia, injuries to the omentum, and uterine bleeding. The review analyzed data from 57 RCTs, which included 9865 participants and evaluated 25 different laparoscopic entry techniques. Most studies focused on low-risk patients, often excluding individuals with a high body mass index (BMI) or a history of prior abdominal surgery. Due to the rarity of serious adverse events and the small sample sizes of the studies, no significant differences were found in the rates of major vascular or visceral complications between the techniques. Open Entry vs. Closed Entry (Veress Needle): Ten RCTs examined vascular injury as an outcome of Veress needle entry, involving 1086 participants and reporting 10 vascular injury events. Four RCTs assessed vascular injury with the open entry technique, involving 376 participants, and reported no vascular injury events. However, these were not direct comparisons. In direct comparisons between Veress needle and open entry techniques, there was insufficient evidence to determine differences in vascular injury rates (Peto OR 0.14, 95% CI 0.00 to 6.82; very low-quality evidence). Similarly, there was insufficient evidence to determine differences in visceral injury (Peto OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.06 to 6.08; very low-quality evidence) or failed entry (Peto OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.14 to 1.42; very low-quality evidence). No studies reported gas embolism or solid organ injury, and mortality was not observed in either group. Direct Trocar Entry vs. Veress Needle Entry: Direct trocar entry was associated with a lower rate of failed entry compared to Veress needle entry (OR 0.24, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.34; moderate-quality evidence). However, there was insufficient evidence to determine differences in vascular injury (Peto OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.18 to 1.96; very low-quality evidence), visceral injury (Peto OR 2.02, 95% CI 0.21 to 19.42; very low-quality evidence), or solid organ injury (Peto OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.06 to 5.65; very low-quality evidence). Mortality and gas embolism were not reported in either group. Direct Vision Entry vs. Veress Needle Entry: There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in vascular injury (Peto OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.05 to 2.85; very low-quality evidence) or visceral injury (Peto OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.34; very low-quality evidence). Other primary outcomes were not reported. Direct Vision Entry vs. Open Entry: There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in visceral injury (Peto OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.00 to 6.50; very low-quality evidence), solid organ injury (Peto OR 6.16, 95% CI 0.12 to 316.67; very low-quality evidence), or failed entry (Peto OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.04 to 4.09; very low-quality evidence). Vascular injury was reported in two studies, with no events in either group. Other primary outcomes were not reported. Radially Expanding (STEP) Trocars vs. Non-Expanding Trocars: There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in vascular injury (Peto OR 0.24, 95% CI 0.05 to 1.21; very low-quality evidence), visceral injury (Peto OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.00 to 6.37; very low-quality evidence), or solid organ injury (Peto OR 1.05, 95% CI 0.07 to 16.91; very low-quality evidence). Other primary outcomes were not reported. Other studies compared a variety of laparoscopic entry techniques, but the evidence was consistently of very low quality. Overall, the review concluded that there is insufficient evidence to recommend one laparoscopic entry technique over another. The only notable finding was that direct trocar entry reduced the likelihood of failed entry compared to Veress needle entry. However, the quality of evidence was generally very low due to small sample sizes, low event rates, and methodological limitations in the included studies.
